One fuzzy navigator for every workspace, agent, project, session, remote, directory, and action in Herdr.

Type what you remember. Navigator decides whether to **focus, create, attach, hand off, invoke, or run**—without making you remember which Herdr surface owns the destination. ```text prefix+t → type → Enter ``` > [!IMPORTANT] > **Upgrading from v0.3.1 or earlier?** Sorry for the one-time breaking rename. Starting with v0.3.2, the plugin ID, binary, config directory, and action prefix are all `herdr-navigator`. See the migration steps below. ## Install ```bash herdr plugin install thanhdat77/herdr-navigator --ref v0.3.3 --yes herdr plugin action invoke herdr-navigator.open ``` If the overlay opens, add a shortcut to `~/.config/herdr/config.toml`. Invoking `open` again focuses the existing Navigator in the current workspace instead of opening a duplicate: ```toml [[keys.command]] key = "prefix+t" type = "plugin_action" command = "herdr-navigator.open" description = "jump to anything" ``` ### Upgrade from v0.3.1 or earlier Sorry for the migration. This completes the rename while the project is still young: ```bash herdr plugin uninstall herdr-picker-plus herdr plugin install thanhdat77/herdr-navigator --ref v0.3.3 --yes herdr server reload-config ``` Replace `herdr-picker-plus` with `herdr-navigator` in your Herdr keybindings. Navigator copies your old plugin config and Jump Back state into the new config directory on first run; the old files are left untouched. Local development links should use `herdr plugin unlink herdr-picker-plus` instead of `uninstall`. Reload Herdr, then press `prefix+t`: ```bash herdr server reload-config ``` ## See it in action

*Source-aware rows keep live status, tabs, and panes aligned at a glance. [Watch the full 17-second demo.](https://github.com/thanhdat77/herdr-navigator/releases/download/v0.3.2/herdr-navigator-v0.3.2-demo.mp4)* A single result list can move between live Herdr state and things that are not open yet: - Type a repo name → focus its open workspace, or create one from a project, zoxide, or configured root. - Type `@idle` or an agent alias → focus that agent pane. - Filter remotes → hand off with Herdr's own `--remote TARGET --handoff` flow. - Select an external integration → run its configured action. ## Why Navigator | Capability | Why it matters | | --- | --- | | **One index across Herdr** | Search workspaces, agents, projects, sessions, remotes, directories, Quick Actions, and integrations together. | | **Action-aware Enter** | Results do not just return paths; they focus, create, attach, hand off, invoke, or run. | | **Reuse first** | Existing workspaces are focused before new ones are created.      5	
     6	Herdr plugins are shareable, executable workflow packages. A plugin can be a
     7	Bash script, JavaScript app, Lua script, Rust binary, or any other argv command
     8	your machine can run. Herdr owns the host surface: installation, manifest

    11	durable state.
    12	
    13	Plugins exist so Herdr can stay lean. The core stays focused on terminal
    14	workspaces, panes, agents, and a stable CLI/socket API. Plugins turn that
    15	existing extension surface into reusable workflows that people can build,
    16	install, and share without adding every workflow to Herdr itself.
    17	
    18	A plugin is not an SDK integration. It is a directory with a
    19	`herdr-plugin.toml` manifest and commands Herdr can launch. Herdr validates the
    20	manifest, injects runtime context, starts the declared commands, and records
    21	logs. The commands call back into Herdr through the CLI or socket when they need
    22	to do more work.
    23	
    24	There is no separate plugin SDK or restricted command set. The entire Herdr CLI
    25	is the plugin API: every command in the [CLI reference](/docs/cli-reference/) is
    26	available to a plugin, and anything you can run as `herdr ...` yourself a plugin
    27	can run too. Most plugins should call Herdr through `HERDR_BIN_PATH`, which
    28	points at the running Herdr binary. That keeps plugins portable across Unix
    29	sockets and Windows named pipes. Use the [socket API](/docs/socket-api/) when
    30	you want to send raw JSON requests yourself.

    32	Runtime action registration and native non-terminal plugin UI are not part of
    33	plugin v1. Actions, event hooks, panes, and link handlers are all declared in
    34	the manifest.

    36	## Trust and security
    37	
    38	A plugin is ordinary code that runs on your machine. When you install or link
    39	one, its build and runtime commands run as your user, with your environment, and
    40	can call the full Herdr CLI — the same as any extension you add to an editor,
    41	shell, or coding agent. That openness is the point, and a little judgment keeps
    42	it safe.
    43	
    44	Install plugins from authors and repositories you trust, and skim what a new one
    45	does first: the `herdr-plugin.toml` manifest and the scripts or binaries it runs.
    46	`herdr plugin install` shows a preview of the source and the commands it will run
    47	in interactive terminals, so you can review before confirming. Use `--yes` for
    48	sources you already trust, and pin `--ref` when you want a specific revision.
    49	
    50	Herdr validates the manifest and keeps each plugin's config and state in its own
    51	directory, but it does not review or sandbox what a plugin does. Third-party
    52	plugins come from their authors, not from Herdr, so they are yours to vet and run
    53	at your own discretion.

    55	## Manifest
    56	
    57	The manifest is the contract between Herdr and the plugin. It declares package
    58	metadata, supported platforms, optional build commands, and the entrypoints
    59	Herdr can run.
